extracted.intended_audience: novelists and fiction writers (especially those working on novel-length projects)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for identifying, designing, balancing, and integrating subplots in a novel so they support the main plot, deepen character, and enhance theme and world-building. Includes types of subplots and practical editing/organization tips.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of a subplot
rubrics_metrics.description: A subplot is a storyline in your novel that is secondary to your main plot. This secondary storyline—or storylines—often run parallel to the main plot and tend to converge toward the climax.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Also includes subplots that run across series installments (plots teased out across multiple books). Treat subplots as having their own beginning, middle, and end even if they feed into the main plot.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary functions/benefits of subplots
rubrics_metrics.description: A good subplot can deepen characterization, make the plot more satisfying or complex, add nuance, genre-blend or place a story within a certain sub-genre, set up great twists for your main plot, tie in foreshadowing for other future events, activate your themes, and enhance world-building.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use subplots as craft tools to plug larger plot holes and to serve multiple narrative purposes rather than existing only for side interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: B/C stories must serve the A plot
rubrics_metrics.description: B and C are your parallel subplots or secondary subplots, but they must come back and serve the A plot.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate subplots by whether they return to and support the main storyline; avoid subplots that never impact or inform the A story.

rubrics_metrics.name: How many subplots to include
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no magic number — include as many subplots as the story requires.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some stories may require very few; multi-volume works, multiple POVs, or stories spanning timelines may need many. Make choices based on narrative needs rather than arbitrary counts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Romantic subplot
rubrics_metrics.description: A romance subplot: a love interest and slow-burn relationship that runs alongside the main plot and can be mapped onto romance beats.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You may use Romancing the Beat or similar beat-mapping to align romance beats with the main plot. If genre-blending, reconsider 'happily ever after' expectations (e.g., romantic tragedy or ambiguous endings). Romance subplots can also drive character development and internal obstacles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character-specific subplots
rubrics_metrics.description: Subplots driven by secondary characters (e.g., a group of rogues whose internal secrets and arcs feed into the primary storyline).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat these as self-contained stories that reveal character and can feed plot reveals; historical examples include Chaucer’s Canterbury Tales where the pilgrimage framework serves character-led sub-stories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-linear subplot (flashbacks/multi-timeframe)
rubrics_metrics.description: Subplots delivered non-linearly (flashbacks or stories spanning generations) that still have a beginning, middle, and end and reveal backstory or causes for present behaviour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use strategically to drip out backstory (e.g., Six of Crows flashbacks) and ensure they are timed to augment current stakes and character motivation rather than stall the main plot.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stakes/up‑the‑suspense subplot (ticking clock)
rubrics_metrics.description: A subplot designed to raise stakes or introduce urgency (for example, blackmail, missing-object problems, or other threats that complicate the protagonist’s objectives).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You can repurpose dangling threads from earlier books (or earlier in the draft) into this kind of subplot to increase suspense and tie loose promises back into the narrative. Ensure the subplot creates meaningful complications and consequences for characters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mirror (parallel) subplot
rubrics_metrics.description: A mirror or parallel subplot where another character faces a conflict similar to the protagonist’s, functioning as a foil to highlight contrasts in reaction or outcome.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use foil dynamics (hero vs villain facing similar obstacles) to create narrative satisfaction when one triumphs and the other fails, highlighting theme and character choice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Frame subplot
rubrics_metrics.description: A subplot that functions as a narrative frame (an interview, a storyteller, or interrupted frame) which also operates as a subplot rather than mere bookends.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure the frame contributes to the story rather than being decorative—examples include Interview With the Vampire (the interview frame) and Frankenstein (interrupted frame as subplot).

rubrics_metrics.name: Map out each subplot (beginning, middle, end)
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify the beginning, middle, and end of each subplot.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat subplots like mini-stories; mapping them helps you see pacing, overlaps with the main plot, and where they should converge with the A plot.

rubrics_metrics.name: Color-code and track subplot presence in scenes
rubrics_metrics.description: Assign each subplot a color and track which scenes touch which subplots so you can see distribution and overlap.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When editing, check which scenes progress which subplots and ensure no subplot disappears for too long unless it intentionally wraps earlier; weave missing subplots into gaps if needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be honest: distinguish subplot from tangent
rubrics_metrics.description: If a subplot could be completely deleted without losing anything to the main plot, it may be a tangent rather than a true subplot.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Either better embed the subplot into the main narrative so it matters, save it for another book, or remove it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Streamline and combine subplots
rubrics_metrics.description: If you have too many subplots, look for ways to combine, simplify, or streamline them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask whether one subplot (e.g., a romance) can also add complications or serve other narrative functions to reduce clutter and increase cohesion.
